extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate students in measure theory, real analysis, or probability; instructors and readers working through exercises
extracted.subtask_description: Working through a textbook chapter on measurability, integration, convergence theorems, expected value, product measures and Fubini — proving results and solving exercises in measure-theoretic probability/analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurability definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A function X : Ω → S is measurable from (Ω, F) to (S, S) iff X^{-1}(B) ≡ {ω : X(ω) ∈ B} ∈ F for all B ∈ S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the basic criterion to verify when declaring a map a measurable map / random variable. Use pre-images: check that inverse images of measurable sets lie in F.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check measurability on a generator
rubrics_metrics.description: If {ω : X(ω) ∈ A} ∈ F for all A in a class A that generates S, then X is measurable (Theorem 1.3.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical verification: it suffices to check pre-images only for a generating class (e.g., half-infinite intervals for R, rectangles for R^d).

rubrics_metrics.name: σ-field generated by a map
rubrics_metrics.description: σ(X) = { {X ∈ B} : B ∈ S } is the smallest σ-field on Ω that makes X measurable (Equation (1.3.1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use σ(X) when discussing measurability relative to minimal information or conditioning; exercises exploit this representation to show Y is measurable wrt σ(X) iff Y = f(X).

rubrics_metrics.name: Useful generators for real-valued maps
rubrics_metrics.description: For (R, R) use {(−∞, x] : x ∈ R} or {(−∞, x) : x ∈ Q}; for (R^d, R^d) use rectangles (a1,b1)×...×(ad,bd) or open sets (Examples 1.3.2–1.3.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose small, convenient generating collections (rationals, rectangles) to simplify measurability checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition preserves measurability
rubrics_metrics.description: If X : (Ω, F) → (S, S) and f : (S, S) → (T, T) are measurable maps then f(X) is measurable (Theorem 1.3.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show f(X) measurable check pre-image: {ω: f(X(ω)) ∈ B} = {ω: X(ω) ∈ f^{-1}(B)}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Random vector measurability via product sets
rubrics_metrics.description: If X1,...,Xn are r.v.'s then (X1,...,Xn) is measurable because for Borel Ai, {(X1,...,Xn) ∈ A1×...×An} = ∩i{Xi ∈ Ai} ∈ F (Theorem 1.3.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verifying measurability of vector-valued maps reduces to verifying measurability of each coordinate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic closure of measurable functions
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is measurable then cX, X^2, sin(X), sums X1+...+Xn, etc., are measurable; sums in particular follow by measurability of the map (x1,...,xn)→x1+...+xn (Theorems 1.3.4–1.3.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build new measurable functions from known ones by composition and measurable multivariate maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and extrema preserve measurability
rubrics_metrics.description: If Xn are measurable then inf_n Xn, sup_n Xn, limsup_n Xn, liminf_n Xn are measurable (Theorem 1.3.7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use countable unions/intersections representations (e.g., {inf Xn < a} = ∪n{Xn < a}) to prove measurability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurability of extended real-valued functions
rubrics_metrics.description: A function from D ∈ F to R* = [−∞,∞] is a random variable if X^{-1}(B) ∈ F for all Borel sets B in the extended real line; R* uses topology generated by [−∞,a), (a,b), (b,∞].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat extended-valued functions with the Borel σ-field on R*; prior closure results extend to this setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-step construction of the integral
rubrics_metrics.description: To define ∫ f dµ follow four steps: (1) simple functions; (2) bounded functions (on finite-measure sets); (3) nonnegative functions; (4) general functions (via positive and negative parts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This constructive sequence is also the blueprint for many proofs (approximate by simple functions, truncate, take monotone limits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral of a simple function
rubrics_metrics.description: If ϕ = Σ_{i=1}^n a_i 1_{A_i} with Ai disjoint and µ(Ai)<∞, then ∫ϕ dµ = Σ_{i=1}^n a_i µ(Ai).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation may not be unique, but the integral is well-defined. Use disjoint decomposition when computing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral of bounded function on finite measure set
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is bounded and vanishes off E with µ(E)<∞, define ∫ f dµ = sup_{ϕ≤f} ∫ϕ dµ = inf_{ψ≥f} ∫ψ dµ where ϕ,ψ are simple and vanish off E (Equation (1.4.1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show sup and inf coincide by approximating f uniformly by simple functions (ψ_n,ϕ_n) and letting mesh→0; this justifies the definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral of a nonnegative function
rubrics_metrics.description: For f ≥ 0 define ∫ f dµ = sup{ ∫ h dµ : 0 ≤ h ≤ f, h bounded, µ({h>0}) < ∞ } (Step 3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approximate nonnegative f by bounded functions with finite support (truncation) and use monotone convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrability and general integral
rubrics_metrics.description: f is integrable iff ∫ |f| dµ < ∞; then define ∫ f dµ = ∫ f+ dµ − ∫ f− dµ (Step 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decompose into positive and negative parts; use linearity where both parts finite (Lemma 1.4.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic integral properties (linearity, monotonicity, absolute value)
rubrics_metrics.description: For appropriate classes of functions: (i) ∫ a f dµ = a ∫ f dµ; (ii) ∫(f+g) = ∫ f + ∫ g; (iii) if f≤g a.e. then ∫ f ≤ ∫ g; (iv) |∫ f| ≤ ∫ |f| (Lemmas 1.4.1–1.4.5, Theorem 1.4.7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These properties are proved first for simple functions and then extended via approximation; they are the axioms you can rely on for computations and inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximation in L1 by simple/step/continuous functions
rubrics_metrics.description: If g is integrable on R then for any ε>0 there exists a simple ϕ with ∫ |g−ϕ| < ε, then a step function q approximating ϕ, and finally a continuous function r approximating q in L1 (Exercise 1.4.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this for density arguments and to justify interchange of limits with integrals in applications (Riemann-Lebesgue lemma etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotone convergence (MCT)
rubrics_metrics.description: If 0 ≤ f_n ↑ f then ∫ f_n dµ ↑ ∫ f dµ (Theorem 1.5.7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MCT to pass limits inside integrals for increasing sequences of nonnegative functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fatou's lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: If f_n ≥ 0 then ∫ liminf_{n→∞} f_n dµ ≤ liminf_{n→∞} ∫ f_n dµ (Theorem 1.5.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Fatou when only lower-semicontinuous (liminf) information is available; it's the cornerstone for dominated convergence proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominated convergence theorem (DCT)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f_n → f a.e., |f_n| ≤ g for all n, and g integrable, then ∫ f_n dµ → ∫ f dµ (Theorem 1.5.8 / 1.6.7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To interchange limit and integral, exhibit an integrable dominating function g and check pointwise a.e. convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounded convergence theorem (finite measure)
rubrics_metrics.description: If E has µ(E)<∞, fn vanish off E, |fn|≤M and fn → f in measure, then ∫ fn → ∫ f (Theorem 1.5.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On finite-measure supports boundedness + convergence in measure suffices (use truncation and measure control).

rubrics_metrics.name: Jensen's inequality (probability measure)
rubrics_metrics.description: If φ is convex and X integrable with φ(X) integrable, then φ(E X) ≤ E φ(X) (Theorem 1.5.1 / 1.6.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use supporting linear function at c=EX to deduce inequality; strict convexity implies equality only when X = EX a.s. (Exercise 1.6.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hölder and Cauchy–Schwarz inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: If p,q ∈ (1,∞) with 1/p+1/q=1 then ∫ |fg| ≤ ||f||_p ||g||_q (Theorem 1.5.2). The case p=q=2 is Cauchy–Schwarz.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these to bound integrals of products and to show L^p spaces are normed; immediate technique: Young's inequality for products and integrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chebyshev / Markov inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: If φ≥0 and i_A = inf{φ(y): y∈A} then i_A P(X∈A) ≤ E(φ(X); X∈A) ≤ E φ(X) (Theorem 1.6.4). Special case φ(x)=x^2 yields a^2 P(|X|≥a) ≤ E X^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply with suitable φ (e.g., φ(x)=|x|^r) to obtain tail bounds; useful for probabilistic estimates and concentration inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected value and variance definitions & properties
rubrics_metrics.description: For probability measure P, EX = ∫ X dP (may be ∞); integrable iff ∫ |X| < ∞. Variance var(X)=E(X−µ)^2=EX^2−(EX)^2 and var(aX+b)=a^2 var(X) (Section 1.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute moments via change-of-variables to distribution; use linearity and moment formula var = EX^2 − (EX)^2 for variance computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change-of-variables / law of the unconscious statistician
rubrics_metrics.description: If X has distribution µ on (S,S) and f measurable with f≥0 or E|f(X)|<∞ then E f(X) = ∫_S f(y) µ(dy) (Theorem 1.6.9).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute expectations of functions of r.v.'s by integrating w.r.t. the distribution measure µ; proven by indicator→simple→nonnegative→integrable progression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximate factorial-moment computations for discrete laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Technique: compute E[X(X−1)...(X−k+1)] for Poisson to get moments; use generating sums and factorial cancellations (Example 1.6.13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use combinatorial moment identities for discrete distributions to derive mean and variance; leverage series manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and uniqueness of product measure (σ-finite case)
rubrics_metrics.description: For σ-finite measure spaces (X,A,µ1) and (Y,B,µ2) there is a unique measure µ on the product σ-algebra F with µ(A×B)=µ1(A)µ2(B) (Theorem 1.7.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct product measure from rectangles and verify countable additivity; σ-finiteness is needed for uniqueness/extension arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fubini / Tonelli condition for iterated integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: If f ≥ 0 or ∫ |f| dµ < ∞ then the iterated integrals equal the full integral: ∫_X (∫_Y f(x,y) dµ2(y)) dµ1(x) = ∫_{X×Y} f dµ = ∫_Y (∫_X f dµ1) dµ2 (Theorem 1.7.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Tonelli for nonnegative f (permit swapping integrals unconditionally) and Fubini for integrable f (|f| integrable). The product-measure framework and σ-finiteness underpin applicability.
